newsitem.title: UK: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - German brokers.
newsitem.headline: THE PROTEUS COLUMN - German brokers.

text.p: This week, the member companies of the Unison broker network will meet in New York to pick up the pieces of their once proud cooperation of independently-minded, mostly privately-owned broking firms. It seems unlikely that German Unison affiliate Jauch & Huebener - the country's largest broker - will remain affiliated with Johnson & Higgins. After all, Marsh McLennan, the new majority owner of Johnson & Higgins, already owns Gradmann Holler, Germany's second largest broker and fierce rival to Jauch & Huebener.

The sudden loss of most of its international network is a hard blow for Jauch & Huebener. And it is not the first such blow dealt to a German broker in recent months: Aon's takeover of Alexander & Alexander last year is making Jaspers Industrie-Assekuranz (JIA) homeless on an international level.

German brokers will have to think hard about their next moves. It would, of course, be possible to find small to medium-sized firms in key markets and build up new networks. It would also be possible to offer oneself for sale to one of the heavyweights.

The first option seems appealing, but only at first sight. An international partnership with a much larger partner (as was the case with Johnson & Higgins and Alexander & Alexander) is helpful, because it ensures a uniform and fast approach to problems on a global scale.

The German brokers were junior partners with regard to international business, but were sure that their clients did get the service they required abroad. A network of companies of about the same size is a very different affair and far more difficult to steer.

The second option, the sale, was taken by the owners (and managers) of Wesselhoeft, Ahlers and Schues, which sold to Aon. It seems unlikely that Jauch & Huebener's shareholders and partners would do the same, they are far too successful in their own right and probably too big to be swallowed easily.

The third option must be, then, for German brokers to build up their own international network of broking firms, in order to serve their industrial customers' needs. What Allianz did in terms of primary insurance and Munich Re as reinsurer will have to be followed by leading German brokers, if they want to stay competitive they will have to buy, especially in America.

But even for Jauch & Huebener, this would prove a tough challenge, both in financial and management terms. A re-arrangement in the German market could help solve that problem. A merger of Jauch & Huebener and JIA or any other form of combining sizeable operations no longer seems impossible, it may be the only way for German brokers to remain a major force in their own market.

THE PROTEUS COLUMN is an insight piece produced by Reuters journalists based on their own research and interpretations. While it aims to be as accurate and incisive as possible, it should not be taken to reflect the views of Reuters Ltd.
